blocks.text: Many schemes have been proposed over the years for classifying organisms into kingdoms. The five-kingdom system of Robert H. Whittaker, which you met in Chapter 1, placed all prokaryotes in a separate kingdom, Monera. In the last decade molecular studies have shown serious flaws in that system, and most biologists now favour the three-domain system, which fits the molecular data better. Bacteria are the prokaryotes classified in a domain of their own, domain Bacteria. This chapter looks at the detailed structure of the bacterial cell and at the importance of bacteria.

blocks.title: Recalling
blocks.text: Robert H. Whittaker proposed the five kingdoms of life: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. The first includes prokaryotes; the other four include eukaryotes.

Bacteria are a diverse group, and all of them have a unicellular prokaryotic organisation: they lack membrane-bounded organelles, including a well-defined nucleus. They have the simplest cellular organisation.

blocks.alt: A rod-shaped bacterial cell cut open lengthwise. From the outside in: capsule, cell wall, cell membrane, then cytoplasm holding ribosomes, a plasmid ring, mesosome infoldings and the nucleoid with its circular DNA. A flagellum extends from one pole and short pili from the surface.
blocks.caption: Structure of a generalised bacterium (original diagram after Figure 2.1).
blocks.long_description: The outer layers are drawn as three concentric lines: a loose capsule outside, the rigid cell wall, and the thin cell membrane inside it. In the cytoplasm the nucleoid is a tangled circular DNA molecule near the centre; small dots are ribosomes; a small circle is a plasmid; infoldings of the membrane are mesosomes. A long wavy flagellum leaves one end of the cell; several short pili stick out of the surface.

blocks.text: The cell wall is a rigid wall around the plasma membrane of the bacterial cell. Its major component is a unique macromolecule called peptidoglycan, or murein. Peptidoglycan is composed of long glycan (polysaccharide) chains cross-linked with short peptide fragments. Its amount differs in different bacteria. The cell wall also contains lipids, which are linked to the peptidoglycan.

The composition of the wall is quite different in Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. The wall of Gram-positive bacteria contains a thick layer of peptidoglycan and has less lipid. The wall of Gram-negative bacteria has a thin layer of peptidoglycan, and it has an outer membrane made of lipopolysaccharides and lipoproteins. This outer membrane makes Gram-negative bacteria resistant to many antibiotics. It contains a protein called porin, which acts like a pore for specific molecules. Gram-negative bacteria also have more periplasmic space (the space between the peptidoglycan layer and the cell membrane) than Gram-positive bacteria.

blocks.alt: Two wall cross-sections side by side. Gram-positive: a thick peptidoglycan layer above the cell membrane. Gram-negative: an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide and porin channels, a wide periplasmic space holding a thin peptidoglycan layer, then the cell membrane.
blocks.caption: Cell wall composition of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (original diagram after Figure 2.3).
blocks.long_description: On the left, the Gram-positive wall: a thick purple peptidoglycan band sits directly on the cell membrane, with only a narrow periplasmic gap. On the right, the Gram-negative wall: an outer membrane studded with lipopolysaccharide and crossed by porin channels, a wide periplasmic space, a thin peptidoglycan layer, and the cell membrane at the bottom.

blocks.title: Gram's staining
blocks.text: Sir Hans Christian Gram devised the technique of Gram's staining. Gram-positive bacteria stain purple because they retain the violet dye. Gram-negative bacteria do not retain the violet dye, so they appear in the original colour of the counterstain.

blocks.text: Some bacteria produce a capsule outside their cell wall. It is a gelatinous layer and gives a sticky character to bacterial colonies.

The cell membrane, or plasma membrane, lies just beneath the cell wall. In bacteria that lack a cell wall (for example mycoplasmas and spiroplasmas) it is the outermost layer. The bacterial cell membrane does not have sterols such as cholesterol in its chemical make-up. At some points the membrane invaginates (folds inwards) to form vesicles, tubules or lamellae in the cytoplasm. These structures are called mesosomes. They are involved in DNA replication and cell division, and they also serve as respiratory centres.

blocks.title: Mesosomes
blocks.text: Infoldings of the bacterial cell membrane that form vesicles, tubules or lamellae in the cytoplasm. They take part in DNA replication and cell division and act as respiratory centres, which is why a bacterium can respire without mitochondria.

The cytoplasm contains dissolved substances and large structures such as the nucleoid, ribosomes and mesosomes. It lacks a cytoskeleton and membrane-bounded organelles. Many ribosomes are freely dispersed in the cytoplasmic matrix and some are loosely attached to the plasma membrane. Bacterial ribosomes are smaller than eukaryotic ribosomes: each sediments at 70S, with a larger 50S subunit and a smaller 30S subunit.

Near the centre of the cytoplasm there is an irregularly shaped dense area, the nucleoid, which contains the DNA. A bacterium possesses a single, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule without attached histones. It is sometimes called the chromosome of the bacterium.

Some bacteria also have small circular, double-stranded, extra-chromosomal DNA molecules called plasmids. Plasmids are self-replicating and can replicate before or after cell division. They carry genes that enable bacteria to resist unfavourable conditions, such as antibiotics. Plasmids also serve as important vectors in genetic engineering: they are used to carry selected genes into bacteria for cloning or for the synthesis of specific proteins.

blocks.prompt: Why does the outer membrane make Gram-negative bacteria resistant to many antibiotics, and what lets specific molecules still cross it?
blocks.explanation: The outer membrane of lipopolysaccharides and lipoproteins acts as an extra barrier outside the thin peptidoglycan layer, so many antibiotics cannot reach their target. Porin proteins in that membrane act as pores for specific molecules.

items: Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotes: no membrane-bounded organelles and no well-defined nucleus.
The cell wall is peptidoglycan (murein): thick in Gram-positive bacteria, thin with an outer membrane (lipopolysaccharides, lipoproteins, porins) in Gram-negative bacteria.
Some bacteria add a gelatinous capsule outside the wall.
The cell membrane lacks sterols; its infoldings, the mesosomes, help DNA replication, cell division and respiration.

The cytoplasm holds 70S ribosomes, the nucleoid with one circular double-stranded DNA without histones, and in some bacteria plasmids that carry resistance genes and serve as vectors in genetic engineering.
